blocks.text: Create Anything You Can Describe

Everyone's creating images and videos for their business, brand, and personal use with AI — and a lot of those viral clips you've scrolled past were made with one tool. If you've been watching from the sidelines, wondering how to get started, it makes that easy. That tool is Kling!

In this guide, you'll learn how to use it — by generating images, videos, and avatars yourself, from your first prompt to a finished output.
What Is Kling AI?
Kling AI is a multimodal creative platform that generates images, videos, and avatars from text prompts and reference images. It runs entirely in a browser.
The Interface

When you open Kling, you'll see your main navigation on a left-hand sidebar. Everything you need to create, find, and manage your work lives here. There are five items to know: Explore, Assets, Generate, Canvas, and All Tools.

• Explore: A feed of other users' generated content. Useful for seeing what Kling produces before you make anything yourself.
  • Assets: Where your own work is stored. Every generation saves here automatically, searchable and downloadable at any time.
  • Generate: Where you create. Access Image Generation, Video Generation, Motion Control, and Avatar from here.
  • Canvas: A multi-layer workspace for projects that combine multiple outputs.
  • All Tools: A full overview of everything Kling offers, including features not visible in the main sidebar.
In the top bar, you'll also see five tools: Image Generation, Video Generation, Motion Control, Kling Canvas, and Avatar 2.0.
Here is what each one handles:

• Image Generation — where you build and test concepts: visual references, mockups, and style explorations before committing to a direction.
  • Video Generation — where you produce the asset: the ad, the clip, the scene, ready for distribution or delivery.
  • Motion Control — where you direct exactly how things move: camera angles, subject trajectory, speed, and direction.
  • Avatar — where you handle delivery: a consistent, reusable character who can speak scripted lines and appear across multiple videos.
Your First Prompt
Let's create your first image in Kling.

blocks.prompt: Ask Kling to generate an image of a horse.

blocks.text: Good! That image is now automatically saved in Kling. When you switch to Video Generation, you can use it as a reference for a more accurate output — or skip it and work from a prompt alone. Here, we'll upload it as a reference to keep the result consistent with what we just generated.

blocks.prompt: Turn the image of a horse into a moving scene.

blocks.text: Here's what a detailed, realistic video looks like when the prompt gives Kling enough to work with. Now let's look at where outputs like these fit in real work.
What Kling Is Used For

Kling works well for both personal projects and professional ones. Need a product photo, a person video, or a branded spokesperson? You don't need a camera, software, or design skills — just open Kling and describe what you need.

Prompting Fundamentals

When most people open Kling for the first time, they type something like "a woman in a café." Kling generates something, but it's probably not what they had in mind. This happens because the prompt never gave it enough to work with.

In this lesson, you'll learn a six-part formula that turns a rough idea into a prompt that gets you what you need — and how to use DeepSeek, built directly into Kling, to get there faster.
Let's Try It
Before we break down in detail what makes a prompt work, let's see the problem firsthand — generate the video and see what comes back.

blocks.prompt: Generate a video in Kling.

blocks.text: Here is how it turned out. It looks good at first glance — but before moving on, let's take a closer look at what's missing and why it matters for the final result.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right. The prompt has a "who" and a "where" but nothing else. Kling has no instruction on how the scene should feel, how it should be lit, or what visual style it should follow. It fills those gaps on its own, which is why the result looks generic rather than intentional. Mood, lighting, style, and atmosphere are what transform a description into a brief.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Physical detail and reference images aren't the issue here. The problem is that the prompt didn't communicate any visual direction. A more detailed description of the woman's appearance still won't tell Kling how the scene should feel or look. That requires mood, lighting, style, and atmosphere, none of which were included.

blocks.question: What is the core issue with the prompt "A woman in a café"?

blocks.text: Yes, Kling generated a video. But the lighting is flat, the mood is neutral, and nothing in the image feels deliberate. To fix this, let's try the 5W1H formula.
The 5W1H Formula
Kling's recommended framework for building detailed prompts centers on 6 questions: Who, What, When, Where, Why, and How.
Here's what each element covers:

• Who — the subject: appearance, age, expression, clothing, defining features.
  • What — the action or state: what the subject's doing, feeling, or how they're positioned.
  • When — the time context: time of day, season, era, or historical period.
  • Where — the setting: location, space, and surrounding environment.
  • Why — the mood and atmosphere: the emotional tone an image should carry.
  • How — the style and execution: photography style, art movement, rendering approach, lens type, or color grading.

Each one adds a specific layer of direction, and together they give Kling everything it needs to generate something usable. 

Now let's go back to the prompt about a woman in a café and rebuild it properly.

blocks.prompt: Turn the vague prompt into something Kling can work with.

blocks.text: Look at the difference. This time, Kling had a full brief to work from. The mood, the lighting, and the style are all there because you told it what you wanted. That's what a structured prompt does.
Use It Flexibly

The 5W1H formula is a great framework, but not a checklist. Depending on your task, you might not need all 6 elements every time. The right approach is to identify which dimensions matter most for the visual you're building and to weight the prompt accordingly.

For example, a landscape prompt might need almost no "Who" or "What". Strong "When", "Where," and "Why" will carry the whole image. Stacking all six can sometimes overload the generation and reduce output quality. Use what serves the image, and leave out what doesn't.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right. When there's no subject in the frame, "Who" and "What" become irrelevant. This image lives or dies on where the scene is set, when it takes place, and why — the emotional atmosphere it carries. Focusing the prompt on those three elements gives Kling what it needs without cluttering the generation.

feedbackIncorrect.text: A landscape without a character doesn't need a "Who" or a "What." Forcing those elements in adds noise rather than direction. The formula works best when you select the elements that serve the image, not when you apply all 6 by default.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right. "Why" is the element that carries emotional weight. Without it, Kling renders the scene accurately but neutrally — correct light, correct location, no feeling. Adding atmospheric language: "melancholic and vast," "the silence before a storm," "a sky heavy with something unresolved" — is what shifts a technically correct image into one that feels like something.

DeepSeek Inside Kling
Kling has a built-in reasoning assistant — DeepSeek. It's accessible directly from the Image and Video Generation workspaces without opening another tool or tab.

So when you have a concept but can't articulate it precisely, DeepSeek fills that gap. 

It applies cinematic, design, and technical language you may not have, turning "A woman in a café" into a generation-ready description with built-in character, setting, atmosphere, and rendering style. Let's try it!

Select the DeepSeek icon inside Kling and type a simple prompt like "A woman in a café." DeepSeek suggests three prompt variations. You can choose the one that looks the most effective for your goal. Click "Use prompt", and it appears in the main field.
A rough idea became a precise, generation-ready brief. This is what Kling produced from it.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right. Give DeepSeek a rough idea, and it returns a prompt with the visual language, mood, and style already built in — no technical vocabulary needed on your end.

feedbackIncorrect.text: DeepSeek doesn't analyze past generations, suggest presets, or work from keyword lists. It works purely on language — taking what you know you want and turning it into a precise, structured brief that Kling can work from.

options.label: It refines your prompt by analyzing similar successful generations
It suggests style presets based on the mood you describe
It rewrites your prompt using keywords that Kling responds to best
It turns rough ideas into structured, generation-ready prompts

blocks.text: And the best part is that DeepSeek lives inside Kling itself. You can enhance your prompt right where you generate, without leaving the platform. Between the 5W1H formula and DeepSeek, you now have two reliable ways to get from a rough idea to a prompt that produces what you had in mind.

  • Use it selectively: Focus on the elements that serve the image and leave out the ones that don't.
  • DeepSeek is built into Kling: Use it to expand rough ideas into structured prompts.

blocks.text: Prompting Fundamentals

When most people open Kling for the first time, they type something like "a woman in a café." Kling generates something, but it's probably not what they had in mind. This happens because the prompt never gave it enough to work with.

In this lesson, you'll learn a six-part formula that turns a rough idea into a prompt that gets you what you need — and how to use DeepSeek, built directly into Kling, to get there faster.
Let's Try It
Before we break down in detail what makes a prompt work, let's see the problem firsthand — generate the video and see what comes back.

blocks.prompt: Generate a video in Kling.

blocks.text: Here is how it turned out. It looks good at first glance — but before moving on, let's take a closer look at what's missing and why it matters for the final result.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right. The prompt has a "who" and a "where" but nothing else. Kling has no instruction on how the scene should feel, how it should be lit, or what visual style it should follow. It fills those gaps on its own, which is why the result looks generic rather than intentional. Mood, lighting, style, and atmosphere are what transform a description into a brief.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Physical detail and reference images aren't the issue here. The problem is that the prompt didn't communicate any visual direction. A more detailed description of the woman's appearance still won't tell Kling how the scene should feel or look. That requires mood, lighting, style, and atmosphere, none of which were included.

options.label: It only describes the subject and location — mood, style, and lighting are all missing
Kling requires a reference image for any scene with a person in it
It needs more physical detail about the woman before anything else can work

blocks.question: What is the core issue with the prompt "A woman in a café"?

blocks.text: Yes, Kling generated a video. But the lighting is flat, the mood is neutral, and nothing in the image feels deliberate. To fix this, let's try the 5W1H formula.
The 5W1H Formula
Kling's recommended framework for building detailed prompts centers on 6 questions: Who, What, When, Where, Why, and How.
Here's what each element covers:

• Who — the subject: appearance, age, expression, clothing, defining features.
  • What — the action or state: what the subject's doing, feeling, or how they're positioned.
  • When — the time context: time of day, season, era, or historical period.
  • Where — the setting: location, space, and surrounding environment.
  • Why — the mood and atmosphere: the emotional tone an image should carry.
  • How — the style and execution: photography style, art movement, rendering approach, lens type, or color grading.

Each one adds a specific layer of direction, and together they give Kling everything it needs to generate something usable. 

Now let's go back to the prompt about a woman in a café and rebuild it properly.

blocks.prompt: Turn the vague prompt into something Kling can work with.

blocks.text: Look at the difference. This time, Kling had a full brief to work from. The mood, the lighting, and the style are all there because you told it what you wanted. That's what a structured prompt does.
Use It Flexibly

The 5W1H formula is a great framework, but not a checklist. Depending on your task, you might not need all 6 elements every time. The right approach is to identify which dimensions matter most for the visual you're building and to weight the prompt accordingly.

For example, a landscape prompt might need almost no "Who" or "What". Strong "When", "Where," and "Why" will carry the whole image. Stacking all six can sometimes overload the generation and reduce output quality. Use what serves the image, and leave out what doesn't.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right. When there's no subject in the frame, "Who" and "What" become irrelevant. This image lives or dies on where the scene is set, when it takes place, and why — the emotional atmosphere it carries. Focusing the prompt on those three elements gives Kling what it needs without cluttering the generation.

feedbackIncorrect.text: A landscape without a character doesn't need a "Who" or a "What." Forcing those elements in adds noise rather than direction. The formula works best when you select the elements that serve the image, not when you apply all 6 by default.

options.label: Useful
Not useful

blocks.question: You want to generate a wide landscape of a stormy coastline at dusk with just the environment and atmosphere.

blocks.text: Good. Knowing which elements to include — and which to leave out — is what separates a focused prompt from an overloaded one. Now let's put the selective approach into practice.

correctTokens: during late dusk with fading light
with a vast and melancholic mood
blocks.prompt: Generate a cinematic coastline landscape only with the 5W1H elements that matter for this image.
tokens: during late dusk with fading light
with a vast and melancholic mood

blocks.text:
A focused three-element prompt produced a cinematic result. 

The framework is flexible precisely because not every image needs every element. It all depends on your idea and the task.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right. "Why" is the element that carries emotional weight. Without it, Kling renders the scene accurately but neutrally — correct light, correct location, no feeling. Adding atmospheric language: "melancholic and vast," "the silence before a storm," "a sky heavy with something unresolved" — is what shifts a technically correct image into one that feels like something.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Time, camera style, and location details all contribute to the landscape, but none convey emotional tone. When an image looks right but feels flat, "Why" is almost always what's missing. Kling can render a coastline at dusk without knowing how that coastline should make the viewer feel. That has to be stated explicitly.

"When" — the time of day wasn't described clearly enough
"How" — the wrong camera style was selected for a landscape
"Where" — the location needed more geographic detail

blocks.question: You generate the coastline landscape, and it looks accurate, but the image feels flat and emotionless. Which element is most likely missing from your prompt?

blocks.text: That's the formula working selectively, each element placed where it earns its place, nothing added for the sake of it. Now, what if you have a rough idea but can't find the right words to describe it?
DeepSeek Inside Kling
Kling has a built-in reasoning assistant — DeepSeek. It's accessible directly from the Image and Video Generation workspaces without opening another tool or tab.

So when you have a concept but can't articulate it precisely, DeepSeek fills that gap. 

It applies cinematic, design, and technical language you may not have, turning "A woman in a café" into a generation-ready description with built-in character, setting, atmosphere, and rendering style. Let's try it!

Select the DeepSeek icon inside Kling and type a simple prompt like "A woman in a café." DeepSeek suggests three prompt variations. You can choose the one that looks the most effective for your goal. Click "Use prompt", and it appears in the main field.
A rough idea became a precise, generation-ready brief. This is what Kling produced from it.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right. Give DeepSeek a rough idea, and it returns a prompt with the visual language, mood, and style already built in — no technical vocabulary needed on your end.

feedbackIncorrect.text: DeepSeek doesn't analyze past generations, suggest presets, or work from keyword lists. It works purely on language — taking what you know you want and turning it into a precise, structured brief that Kling can work from.

options.label: It refines your prompt by analyzing similar successful generations
It suggests style presets based on the mood you describe
It rewrites your prompt using keywords that Kling responds to best
It turns rough ideas into structured, generation-ready prompts

blocks.question: What makes DeepSeek useful inside Kling?

blocks.text: And the best part is that DeepSeek lives inside Kling itself. You can enhance your prompt right where you generate, without leaving the platform. Between the 5W1H formula and DeepSeek, you now have two reliable ways to get from a rough idea to a prompt that produces what you had in mind.

• Vague prompts produce vague results: Kling needs direction, not just a subject and location.
  • The 5W1H formula: Who, What, When, Where, Why, and How each adds a specific layer of direction.
  • Use it selectively: Focus on the elements that serve the image and leave out the ones that don't.
  • DeepSeek is built into Kling: Use it to expand rough ideas into structured prompts.

blocks.text: Unit 1 Completed!

Good work! You know what Kling is, how it works, and how to write structured prompts that get you what you had in mind. 

Now it's time to go deeper — Unit 2 puts each tool to work, starting with Image Generation. Let's go!
From Idea to Image

You already know how to write a solid prompt. Today, let's see what it produces. A prompt that took seconds to write can turn into a detailed image, a styled illustration, or a full set of consistent visuals.

In this lesson, you'll learn how to use Kling's Image Generation to produce visuals from text, edit them, and keep everything visually consistent across an entire project.
What You Can Generate

The possibilities of Kling's Image Generation are endless: creating product mockups, lifestyle scenes, concept drafts, 3D renders, illustrations, logos, and more — for personal projects and professional work.

Let's start with the basics and work through each capability step by step.
Before generating, take a look at the Image Generation settings. At the bottom, you'll find three options:

• Mode: 1K SD or 2K HD
  • Ratio: from 9:16 to 21:9
  • Output: how many images to generate at once
Adjust these based on what you need: a square for social, a widescreen for film, or multiple outputs to compare variations.
Your First Image Generation
Time to try it out! Generate an image, edit it with a text instruction, then transform its style entirely.

blocks.prompt: Ask Kling to generate an image of a toy car.

blocks.text: Now try changing something in the toy car image without touching anything else.
Text-Based Editing

Kling lets you edit a generated image by typing a plain instruction. Add an object, remove one, swap a color, change a detail, and the model applies the change while preserving the original lighting, style, and texture.

correctTokens: Change the car color to yellow
blocks.prompt: Change the color of the toy car using a single text instruction.
tokens: Change the car color to yellow

blocks.text: The color changed, while the style, lighting, and background remained the same. That's what text-based editing does.
Image-Based Editing

Text instructions work well when you know exactly what to change. But sometimes the result you're after is harder to describe in words, such as a specific texture, a finish, or a visual feel. That's when you upload a reference image and let Kling match the style visually rather than interpret it from text.

You can describe a style directly in your prompt or use Kling's built-in Styles library to pick one visually. Either way, Kling applies it to your image while preserving its shape, proportions, and composition.
Imagine you want to give the car a kids' toy feel by applying a style reference. Let's see how the image changes depending on which style you pick.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right. "Knit Fabric" style gives the car a soft, handmade feel — perfect for a kids' toy. The texture changes the surface without touching the shape.

feedbackIncorrect.text: "Wasteland" style pulls the image toward something gritty and dark — the opposite of what a kids' toy needs. The style you pick matters as much as the subject itself.

options.label: Style
Wasteland Sci-fi
Knit Fabric

blocks.prompt: Identify which style reference fits a kids' toy aesthetic and replace the default option.
blocks.template: Apply [Style] to the toy car image
blocks.title: Pick the Right Style

blocks.text: Excellent!
This is where Image Generation goes deeper. Kling reads the style of an image — the colors, texture, and composition — and applies it to a new one while keeping the original structure.
Let's try a more practical task. Imagine you need to create an interior design layout for a living room. Start with a simple description with a Design Draft Style, then transform it into a 3D model.

correctTokens: with a sofa, coffee table, shelving unit, and a plant
blocks.prompt: Ask Kling to generate a living room interior layout.
tokens: with a sofa, coffee table, shelving unit, and a plant

blocks.text: Great! You have a clean living room layout. Now you can use it as a reference to transform it into a realistic 3D model with a single instruction.

blocks.prompt: Transform the living room layout into a realistic 3D-style render.

blocks.text: Great Work!

The flat layout was rendered as a photorealistic 3D scene with the same proportions and furniture placement. That's how you can use style transformation: take any image and shift how it looks without changing what's in it.

feedbackCorrect.text: Style transformation works on what already exists — the content stays exactly as it is, and only the visual execution changes. That applies whether you're shifting a flat illustration to a 3D render, a sketch to a painted finish, or a rough layout to a polished visual.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Style transformation doesn't generate new content, pull references from online, or rearrange anything. It takes what's already in the image and changes how it looks — nothing more, nothing less. The moment you change the content, you're no longer transforming style; you're generating something new.

options.label: It changes how an image looks without changing what's in it
It adjusts colors and composition based on current design trends
It searches for similar styles online and applies their aesthetic to your image
It generates a new version of the image based on your style preferences from scratch

blocks.question: How does style transformation help you in a real-world task?

blocks.text: You've seen how style transformation works on a single image. Let's look at what happens when you need that same visual consistency across multiple outputs at once.
Multi-Reference Input

When you need multiple outputs to look consistent, upload your reference images, and Kling aligns every generation to them — up to 10 images at once. Let's generate a logo to use as our first reference.

blocks.prompt: Ask Kling to create a minimal brand logo.

blocks.text: Now upload the logo and a mug photo as references, and generate branded product visuals from them in the same session.

correctTokens: a mug and a packaging box
blocks.prompt: Upload a logo image and generate two branded product visuals.
blocks.template: Keep [subject] unchanged and generate [objects], primarily [color treatment]
tokens: a mug and a packaging box

blocks.text: Perfect!

Both outputs arrived visually consistent — same logo, color treatment, and brand feel — without any manual alignment. You generated the reference in the same session, and Kling carried it through the outputs that followed.
You can now generate, edit, transform, and maintain consistency across a full image session!

• Text-based editing: Changes one element without touching anything else. Use it when the image is close but not quite right.
  • Image-based editing: Upload a reference, and it applies the visual language directly.
  • Style transformation: Convert the rendering approach with one instruction — knit texture to photorealistic, sketch to 3D render, without rebuilding anything from scratch.
  • Multi-reference input: Upload once, stay consistent across the entire session.
blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text:
You've gone from a text prompt to a styled image, an edited detail, a 3D render, and a fully consistent brand set — all without leaving Kling.

In the next lesson, those same images will start moving! Video Generation brings in camera control, multi-shot structure — and everything you've learned about prompting applies directly. Let's try it.

Turning Ideas Into Moving Scenes

You already know how to generate images, but you can also animate them in Kling.

In this lesson, you'll learn how to get from a still image to a finished video clip straight from your browser.
Two Ways Into a Video
Kling's Video Generation has two entry points:

• Text-to-Video generates a moving scene from a written description. Useful when you're starting from an idea.
  • Image-to-Video takes a still image you already have and animates it into a clip. Useful when the composition and lighting are already right, and you just want it to move.
Video Settings
Before you start generating them, there are four settings to configure in Kling:

• Mode
  • Length
  • Video Ratio
  • Number of Outputs

Those settings apply to every generation you run — whether you start from text or an image. You can customize them depending on what the clip needs: a longer duration for a full scene, a shorter duration for a quick cut, a vertical ratio for mobile, or a widescreen aspect ratio for a cinematic feel.

Let's put them to use, starting with a text description.

Building AI Avatars

Ever wanted a spokesperson, a character, or just a face to bring your idea to life without filming anyone? That's exactly what Avatar Generation is for. 

In this lesson, you'll learn how to create a digital human, give it a voice, and place it in a scene that looks production-ready from the start.
Avatar Generation
Kling's Avatar Generation creates a digital human character from a written description or a reference photo.

In Avatar, you'll find two starting points. Avatar Library gives you ready-made presets for common formats — Vlog, Talking Head, Podcast — so you can get started without building a character from scratch.
Or you can build one yourself using a prompt and AI Image feature, customizing gender, age, skin tone, and generating a full character description from your own inputs. Let's create one!

blocks.prompt: Generate a digital human avatar in Kling.
tokens: with dark hair and sharp features

blocks.text: Speech

With your avatar saved, go to Speech in the left panel and type in what you want your character to say. Set the language, accent, and tone, and the audio adjusts automatically. Try typing this line: "Welcome to our latest product launch. Everything you'll see today was built with one goal: to make your workflow faster, cleaner, and easier to manage from day one."

blocks.prompt: Assign a scripted line to the avatar you just created in Speech.

blocks.text: The mouth movements and facial expressions followed the script without any manual adjustment.

feedbackCorrect.text: An avatar works anywhere you need a consistent, speaking human presence — product launches, course content, blogs, and recurring video series. Once saved, the same face and voice are available for every project that follows without rebuilding anything.

feedbackIncorrect.text: An avatar is a speaking character — it needs a role where a consistent human presence delivers content directly. Using it as a background element or animating a logo are visual tasks that don't involve a speaking presenter, which is what the avatar is built for.

blocks.question: What can you use your saved avatar for?

blocks.text: You can use one avatar for multiple uses: vlogs, podcasts, product clips, or course modules. Kling also lets you place two or more avatars in the same scene, each with their own dialogue, animated independently as they speak.
Multi-Character Scenes
Let's create a male character to pair with the one you just built. Follow the same process.
Now, set your first avatar as the start frame and your second as the end frame in Video Generation. Then describe the scene in the prompt: who speaks first and what they say.
You got two avatars in one scene from a single prompt. Kling tracked which character was speaking and animated each one independently.
Cross-Session Consistency

For the last step, every avatar you generate in Kling is saved to your Assets. The same facial structure, expressions, and visual identity are locked in. You can reopen the avatar in any future session, and it looks identical to the first time you generated it.

Kling for Filmmakers

Today, imagine you have a screenplay and need to show your cinematographer, actors, and investors what the film looks like. 

In this lesson, you'll learn how to use Kling to turn a script into visual references, scene stills, and animatics in a single session.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right. A generated scene image gives everyone on the crew something concrete to look at and react to before any equipment is hired or any location is booked. That's where Kling fits in at this stage.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Written descriptions, borrowed film references, and waiting until the scout all leave room for misinterpretation. A generated image puts everyone on the same page visually, at the earliest and cheapest point in the process.

Generate a scene image from your script description: location, lighting, character position, and mood

blocks.question: You need to give your crew a clear visual idea of a scene before the shoot. What's the most practical first step?

blocks.text: Step 1: Generate a Scene Image
Kling's Image Generation takes your script description: location, lighting, character positions, and mood, and turns it into a reference frame your whole crew can look at and respond to.
Let's make one. Describe a scene from your script and generate the image that goes to your cinematographer.

blocks.prompt: Generate a reference image from a script description in Kling Image.

blocks.text: You have an image with location, mood, lighting, and character position. If you need to compare two different lighting setups before committing, you can generate both as separate stills and decide before anything gets locked in.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right. The value is in the timing: creative decisions made at the image stage cost nothing to change. The same decision made after equipment is hired, or a crew is on set, costs money. Kling moves that conversation earlier in the process.

feedbackIncorrect.text: A scene still doesn't replace a cinematographer, produce final footage, or reduce what a crew needs to think about on set. It gives everyone a shared visual reference before production starts — where the real savings are, in time and cost.

options.label: It produces a final-quality image that can be used directly in the film
It lets you resolve visual decisions before any crew, equipment, or location costs are committed
It speeds up the shoot day by giving the crew less to think about on set
It replaces the need for a director of photography on the project

A still shows the look, while a moving clip shows the feel: how the camera travels and the character moves through the frame, and how long the scene breathes. 

Upload your still into Kling's Image-to-Video, describe the motion, and you have a clip your producer and director of photography can watch.

Now that the still and motion are covered, let's lay out the full scene.

Custom Multi-Shot lets you specify every shot in a scene individually: framing, angle, transition. Each one comes back as a moving cinematic clip. Let's build it with the generated video.

Storyboard done! You now have a visual sequence that shows how the film looks and flows shot by shot. 

Next, let's go one level deeper: directing exactly how a camera and a character move.
Direct Precise Movement With Motion Control

Motion Control lets you define exactly how a character moves. Upload a reference action video or pick a preset from Motion Library, add a character image, and Kling mimics that movement with your character's face and body.
Let's try the workflow:

1. Choose preset from Motion Library showing the movement you want to copy.
  2. Upload the character image alongside.
  3. Click Generate.
Perfect!
The preset video set the motion, and your character moved through the frame in the same way. You can choose or upload any reference action video that aligns with your vision.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right. Motion Control is built for this: you upload a reference video showing the movement you want, bind your character to it, and Kling replicates that motion with your character's face and body in one continuous clip.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The reference video is what defines the motion. Without it, Kling has no specific movement to replicate and will interpret the action freely.

Another way you can use Kling in a professional context is in education. Whether you're building an onboarding course, a training module, or a lecture series, Kling gives you a production team of one.

The Challenge
Say you need to build a five-module onboarding course. You can do all of it without a camera or a studio. But how do you make sure the course looks and feels like a single cohesive experience?
The answer is the avatar. Generate your presenter once, save it, and reuse it across every module. Let's build it step by step.
Step 1: Create the Avatar Instructor
Generate your presenter in Kling's Avatar workspace: set the appearance, choose the voice, and save it. That character becomes the instructor for every module.
